from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

sections.title: The Intuitive Paradox (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive concept: Can a 1D line perfectly cover a 2D area? Start with the prerequisite: The concept of topological dimension vs. Lebesgue covering dimension. Explain that while a line is 1D, it can have an infinite length that 'fills' space.
sections.example: Visualize a single, infinitely long piece of yarn being folded back and forth until it completely covers a square tile.

sections.title: The Recursive Anatomy: Peano & Hilbert (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Explain the construction process using Iterative Function Systems (IFS). Focus on the 'divide and conquer' strategy: sub-dividing a square into 4 quadrants and connecting them to ensure continuity.
sections.example: Show a Hilbert Curve animation: Start with an 'n' shape. Replace each straight segment with a smaller version of the whole, demonstrating the recursive fractal nature.

sections.title: Mathematical Properties: Continuity vs. Differentiability (2:00-3:15)
sections.content: Highlight the key mathematical tension: These curves are continuous functions, yet they are nowhere differentiable. Explain that they map the interval [0,1] onto the unit square [0,1]x[0,1] in a surjective (onto) manner.
sections.example: Use a 'Pixel Map' visual: An animation showing a single moving dot traversing every single pixel in a 1024x1024 screen without ever lifting its 'pen'.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Data Locality (3:15-4:30)
sections.content: Transition to utility. Explain how these curves preserve 'spatial locality.' By mapping 2D/3D data into 1D, we can store multi-dimensional data in 1D databases while keeping neighbors close to each other.
sections.example: An animation of a Cache Controller (a robot character) trying to find memory addresses. Compare the inefficient 'Row-major' search vs. the efficient 'Hilbert Curve' search.

sections.title: Conclusion and Further Exploration (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize that space-filling curves are not just mathematical curiosities but tools for data compression, image processing, and path optimization.
sections.example: Show a brief montage of a drone using a space-filling path to scan a field efficiently without retracing steps.
